extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, research press officers, and researchers navigating journal embargo policies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria about how journal embargoes (especially Nature's) interact with conference presentations, preprints, newsroom coverage, and researcher/press communications. Useful for press officers, authors, and reporters deciding what may be reported before formal publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingelfinger Rule / prior publication
rubrics_metrics.description: For a journal to publish a study, its results can't have appeared elsewhere, with the exception of limited conference presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the traditional Ingelfinger Rule (named for the NEJM editor) and notes that critics say it can stifle communication. The post uses this as background to question whether Nature would publish a paper after a news story had already reported on its findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature: conference presentations and preprints are not prior publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature journals do not wish to hinder communication between scientists. For that reason, different embargo guidelines apply to work that has been discussed at a conference or displayed on a preprint server and picked up by the media as a result. (Neither conference presentations nor posting on recognized preprint servers constitute prior publication.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Nature's embargo policy and an editorial: if Nature journalists or others hear results at a meeting or find them on a preprint server, coverage is fair game and not considered breaking Nature's embargo. This distinguishes formal publication from public presentations/preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author guidance: permitted scholarly communication but restrict press engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate with other researchers as much as you wish, whether on a recognised community preprint server, on Nature Precedings, by discussion at scientific meetings (publication of abstracts in conference proceedings is allowed), in an academic thesis, or by online collaborative sites such as wikis; but do not encourage premature publication by discussion with the press (beyond a formal presentation, if at a conference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may share work via conferences, preprints, theses, and collaborative sites, but must avoid actively promoting media coverage or informal press discussions that would encourage premature publication. The exception allowed is formal presentation at a conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: News/editorial independence and conflict-of-interest management
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature’s news team are editorially independent and do not receive special treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges potential conflict of interest when journals host news sections reporting on studies they publish (e.g., Nature, Science). The post suggests this is a real concern but one that can be managed; transparency and adherence to embargo rules are implied safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo remains until journal publication; availability of full data/methods matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper was still under embargo until we published on Sunday. The full data and methodology were not in the public domain and the researchers had not spoken with the press about the work except under embargo conditions in the week before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that prior media mentions of conference presentations do not necessarily lift an embargo: the journal considered the paper under embargo until formal publication because full data/methods were not publicly available and the authors had not freely spoken to the press outside embargo terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open meeting presentations may be reported immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: If results are presented at a meeting open to the public, anyone could report on them starting when they were presented; coverage based on such presentations is fair game even if it precedes the paper's publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a March 23 public presentation meant reporters could lawfully report the findings immediately; Nature's later story did not make earlier reporting a breach of Nature's embargo. This establishes that public conference content can be covered by media without violating the journal's embargo policies (per Nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientists may answer journalists' factual queries but must not promote coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor is it a violation if scientists respond to journalists’ queries in ensuring that the facts are correct — so long as they don’t actively promote media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes permissible factual clarification (responding to queries to ensure accuracy) from active efforts to promote or encourage media coverage, which would contravene embargo guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference hosts should manage broadcast/posting permissions; speakers must balance embargo obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts need to carefully manage permissions from speakers over what material from live presentations they may broadcast or subsequently post online; speakers need to balance this with their various journal embargoes for any 'in press' work they have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYAS example: hosts often cannot predict or control which attendees are media (some are members and may not self-identify), so hosts have limited control over who reports from sessions. This is an operational caution about controlling premature dissemination.
